items.prompt: Which one shows what a single state looks like when things go right?
items.explanation: A file is a snapshot of one state. A spec covers every state, value and edge case.

items.prompt: Which one tells an engineer what to build for every state and edge case?
items.explanation: A spec is the instruction set. A screenshot or file only shows what was drawn.

items.prompt: Sam built what he could see and left out the empty state. What is the most likely reason?
choices: He ignored the design on purpose
He was in a hurry to finish up
Nobody drew it, so he could not see it
items.explanation: Engineers build from what is visible. An undrawn state is invisible, not refused.

items.prompt: What does an engineer usually do when the file has a gap?
choices: Stops work until the designer replies
items.explanation: Under a deadline a gap gets a guess made from whatever is visible.

items.prompt: Priya's frame was accurate for the default state. Does that make it a complete handoff?
items.explanation: Accuracy of one state is not coverage of all states.

items.prompt: Reinterpretation of a design is usually caused by what?
items.explanation: It is typically an honest attempt to fill a real gap, not bad intent.

items.prompt: A message says "ready to build" with one frame attached. What is missing?
items.explanation: Other states, exact values, motion and reasoning are not in a single frame.

items.prompt: A spec removes what, without removing the engineer's judgment?
choices: Guessing with nothing to go on
The need to have a design file
items.explanation: Judgment still applies; the spec only stops guesses made in the dark.

items.prompt: A designer says "the file is ready, every pixel is exactly right." What question does that leave open?
choices: Whether the frame was exported at a high enough resolution for engineering
Whether every state and value an engineer needs is included
Whether the typeface was approved by the brand team
Whether the layers are named tidily enough for the engineer to find them
items.explanation: Pixel accuracy covers the state shown. It cannot say whether the other states exist.
items.reference:
A design file versus a spec
File: shows one state when all goes well
Spec: says what to build in every state
Gap: engineer fills it with a guess
Why: a file is a snapshot; a spec is an instruction set an engineer can build from without asking.
items.learnMore:
A design file versus a spec

A file can be exact about the one state it shows and still be an incomplete handoff. Completeness is measured by what an engineer needs across every situation, not by the fidelity of what happens to be drawn.

Common mistake

Treating "every pixel is right" as "ready to build". Accuracy of the drawn part says nothing about the undrawn parts.
items.reflection: Think of instructions you gave someone that looked complete to you. What did they have to guess, and what did you know that never left your head?

items.prompt: Two handoffs show the same accurate default frame. Handoff A adds all states and values; B adds nothing. After the build, which statement is justified?
choices: Both are equally buildable, since the frame is identical
B is better because it leaves engineers freedom to decide
A removes guesses that B forces the engineer to make
A is worse, since extra material slows engineers
items.explanation: The shared frame is the same; the difference is the gap B leaves for guessing.

items.prompt: Which state shows what a screen looks like when there is nothing to display?
items.explanation: The empty state covers a list or cart with no content.

items.prompt: Which state appears while the app waits for a response?
items.explanation: Loading is the waiting state.

items.prompt: Which state confirms an action worked?
items.explanation: Success confirms completion, sometimes with motion.

items.prompt: Which state tells the user something failed and how to recover?
items.explanation: The error state explains the failure and the next step.

items.prompt: How many states did Priya design for checkout?
items.explanation: Default, loading, success, error and empty: five.

items.prompt: How many of those five did the handoff frame show?
items.explanation: Only default and loading were in the frame.

items.prompt: Which states are easiest to forget?
items.explanation: Nobody asks about them, so they silently go missing.

items.prompt: Who can build a state that no one drew?
choices: Only the designer, and only once
items.explanation: An undrawn state has no input to build from.

items.prompt: A cart arrives at checkout with zero items. The handoff has no empty state. What happens at build time?
choices: The engineer pauses the build and asks the designer at once
The cart acts as if it had an item, or shows nothing
The build fails its checks and cannot be released
The default state is hidden automatically by the framework
items.explanation: Without a drawn empty state the engineer has nothing to build, so the screen behaves by accident.
items.reference:
Covering every state
Default: drawn
Loading: drawn
Success, error, empty: easy to forget
Why: each state is a separate thing to build, and nobody can build one that was never drawn.
items.learnMore:
Covering every state

Besides the happy path, a screen usually has loading, success, error and empty versions. The ones nobody asks about, error and empty, are exactly the ones that go missing.

Common mistake

Assuming the engineer will "obviously" think of the empty or error case. They build what the file shows.
items.reflection: Pick a screen you use daily. What does it show when there is nothing to show, or when something fails? Who decided that?

items.prompt: Which pair of states most needs deliberate attention because no one tends to request them?
items.explanation: Error and empty are off the happy path, so they are the ones people forget to draw.

items.prompt: What is a design token?
choices: A named value shared across screens
A secret login key for the design tool
A coloured sticker placed on a frame
items.explanation: A token is a named value defined once and reused.

items.prompt: Priya intended 24px, Sam shipped 16px. What kind of error is that?
choices: A bug in the code logic
items.explanation: He read a number off a visual, and measurement drifts.

items.prompt: Which reading method cannot drift?
items.explanation: A token is looked up, not measured.

items.prompt: If a token changes from 24px to 28px, what happens to everything that reads it?
items.explanation: A token is a single source that changes propagate from.

items.prompt: The Figma inspector reports a gap. What does it really show?
items.explanation: It measures the layer, not the intended rule.

items.prompt: What does an engineer do with a token instead of measuring?
items.explanation: They read the defined value.

items.prompt: A hundred buttons read one token. How many true values exist?
items.explanation: All share the token's single value.

items.prompt: Which is the weakest way to get a spacing value?
items.explanation: Eyeballing drifts silently with nothing to catch it.

items.prompt: Two screens should share 24px spacing. One reads spacing-lg, the other hard-codes 16px. Later the token becomes 28px. What is the result?
choices: Both stay at 24px until someone edits each screen by hand later
Both become 16px because the smaller value always wins on conflict
One becomes 28px; the other stays at 16px
items.explanation: Only the screen that reads the token follows the change; a typed value is a private copy.
items.reference:
Design tokens
Eyeball: drifts silently
Inspector: measures one layer's accident
Token: named, shared, cannot drift
Why: a token is read, not measured, so every use of it stays in sync.
items.learnMore:
Design tokens

Reading a pixel value off a visual is measurement, and measurement drifts. A token such as spacing-lg = 24px is a named value defined once; the engineer looks it up, so a hundred uses share one true value.

Common mistake

Trusting the inspector's number as the intended rule. It reports what this layer computed, which may not be what the designer meant.
items.reflection: Where in your own work do you copy a number by hand instead of naming it once? What breaks the day it needs to change?

items.prompt: An engineer measures a layer in the inspector and gets 16px; the designer meant 24px. Why is inspector reading weaker than a token?
choices: It reports this layer's computed result, not the intended rule
Inspectors round every value to the nearest ten
Inspectors only ever report colours and never report any spacing
Layers never store a spacing value that an inspector could read
items.explanation: The inspector shows an accident of layout; a token states the intent.

items.prompt: Is design QA best as a final gate or an early loop?
choices: An early loop during the build
It is not needed at all
items.explanation: An early loop lets drift go back into open work.

items.prompt: Who ideally does design QA?
choices: Someone who knows the original intent
Anyone who has never seen the design
Only the engineer who built the screen
items.explanation: QA needs the original intent to compare against.

items.prompt: What does design QA compare?
choices: Build and spec, side by side
items.explanation: It checks built output against what was specified.

items.prompt: Does catching a gap late change how many gaps exist?
choices: No, it changes the fix cost
items.explanation: The gaps come from the handoff, not from timing.

items.prompt: A gap found 2 days before launch is usually what compared with 30 days before?
items.explanation: Later means reopening merged, reviewed work.

items.prompt: A spacing value swap versus new empty-cart logic: which is quicker to fix late?
items.explanation: A value substitution adds no new code paths.

items.prompt: Where does a failed QA check go in the loop?
items.explanation: The loop routes drift back while the build is open.

items.prompt: If QA is only a pre-launch gate, what is lost?
choices: A cheap place to route a fix
items.explanation: A late gate has nowhere cheap to send a fix.

items.prompt: Using the unit's illustrative curve, roughly how many hours does a gap cost at 14 days before launch versus 2 days before?
items.explanation: The curve gives about 19.4 h at 14 days and 79.9 h at 2 days; cost rises as launch nears.
items.reference:
When design QA runs
30 days out: about 4 h of rework
14 days out: about 19 h
2 days out: about 80 h
Why: the same gap costs more the later it is found, because it means reopening merged, reviewed work.
items.learnMore:
When design QA runs

Design QA works as a loop during the build, so a drift found goes straight back into open work. As a late gate it has nowhere cheap to send a fix. The cost curve in the unit's demo is illustrative: steep as launch nears.

Common mistake

Believing late QA finds more bugs. The count is the same; the cost and kind of each fix change.
items.reflection: In a task of yours, when do you first check the result against the original intent? What would change if you checked halfway?

items.prompt: QA is moved from the day before launch to mid-build. The same five gaps are found either way. What changes?

The designer no longer needs to review the built screen
items.explanation: The count is fixed by the handoff; timing changes the cost and category of each fix.

items.explanation: Nobody can build from a state that was not drawn.

items.prompt: The success animation became a static checkmark. What was missing?
items.explanation: A durable motion note would have replaced a three-week-old memory.

items.prompt: Spacing shipped at 16px, not 24px. What was missing?
items.explanation: spacing-lg = 24px, read instead of measured.

items.prompt: The wrong red was used. What was missing?
items.explanation: A named colour token removes the guess.

items.prompt: Design QA found gaps only on day 28. What was missing?
choices: A larger screen to test on
items.explanation: QA built into the sprint finds gaps while they are cheap.

items.prompt: Did the five gaps need more design skill from Priya?
items.explanation: Each gap traces to one missing artifact, not a skill gap.

items.prompt: Which gap was a measurement error rather than a judgment call?
items.explanation: Sam read a layer value; he did not choose 16px.

items.prompt: What fixes a verbal-only detail?
choices: Writing it down where it can be checked
items.explanation: A written note does not depend on anyone's memory.

items.prompt: A motion detail was described aloud to five people three weeks before the build. Which artifact would have carried it?
choices: A larger Figma frame showing the same default state again
A written motion note with a short reference
A second design review weeks earlier
A faster build server for the engineering team to use
items.explanation: A written note is durable; spoken details depend on memory.
items.reference:
Mapping each gap to its missing artifact
Empty state: draw the state
Animation: motion note
Colour, spacing: token reference
Late QA: mid-build check-in
Why: each gap traces to one specific missing artifact, not to a lack of skill or care.
items.learnMore:
Mapping each gap to its missing artifact

In the incident every drifted detail maps to a nameable absent artifact: an undrawn state, an unwritten motion note, a missing token reference, a QA scheduled too late. Fix what is handed off and when, not who holds which skill.

Common mistake

Blaming the engineer's care or the designer's talent. The five gaps needed neither more skill nor more effort.

items.prompt: Should a spec document every wrapper element's padding?
choices: Yes, but only in a footnote
items.explanation: Over-specifying buries what matters.

items.prompt: The key test for adding an annotation is what?
choices: Could an engineer reasonably decide differently?
Is the designer free to write it today?
Is the screen colourful enough to show it?
items.explanation: Annotate real decisions with a plausible alternative.

items.prompt: A value repeats on ten screens. Annotate or skip?
items.explanation: Repetition means consistency matters.

items.prompt: A tooltip's padding is local and nobody will scrutinise it. Annotate or skip?
items.explanation: A local one-off rarely deserves a dedicated annotation.

items.prompt: A disabled versus hidden button changes what?
items.explanation: It affects what the user can do, so it needs stating.

items.prompt: Why can over-specifying backfire?
items.explanation: A document that cannot be skimmed for what matters gets skimmed anyway.

items.prompt: Is a state like empty or error worth specifying?
choices: Yes, nobody will think to ask
Only if time remains at the end
items.explanation: These are the states people forget.

items.prompt: Is the already-visible default state worth heavy annotation?
items.explanation: If the frame already makes it clear, extra notes add little.

items.prompt: Which item most clearly deserves an annotation?
choices: Padding on a one-off tooltip that few people will ever see
The default frame's obvious layout, already clear from the picture
Whether a button is disabled or hidden when the cart is empty
The border width on one rarely seen icon in a settings page
items.explanation: Disabled versus hidden changes behaviour, a real decision with alternatives.
items.reference:
Calibrating spec detail
Repeats across screens: annotate
Changes behaviour: annotate
Local and one-off: skip
Why: annotate where an engineer could reasonably decide differently, and skip what has no real alternative.
items.learnMore:
Calibrating spec detail

More spec is not automatically better. Over-annotating buries the decisions that matter and trains engineers to skim. The test is whether a real decision exists that someone could make differently than the designer intends.

Common mistake

Treating the incident as a case for specifying everything. A spec nobody reads closely fails like a missing one.

items.prompt: A designer, burnt by the incident, annotates every internal element. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: Engineers skim, and key decisions get lost in the noise
Every drift disappears because every element is now documented
The design file shrinks because annotations replace the frames
items.explanation: A spec that cannot be skimmed for what matters stops being read closely.

items.learnMore:
Calibrating spec detail

More spec is not automatically better. Over-annotating buries the decisions that matter and trains engineers to skim. The test is whether a real decision exists that someone could make differently than the designer intends.
